task: Use Cambridge Dictionary to understand the use of articles ('a', 'an', 'the') in English Grammar, including examples of usage with both countable and uncountable nouns.
answer: Final Response: Using the Cambridge Dictionary British Grammar "A/an and the" page (https://dictionary.cambridge.org/grammar/british-grammar/articles): Articles define a noun as specific or unspecific. (1) a/an is the indefinite article: it refers to something mentioned for the first time or to any member of a class, and is used only with singular countable nouns, e.g. "I have a sister and a brother", "That was an excellent meal". (2) the is the definite article: it is used when the reader/listener knows which thing is meant; it can be used with singular and plural countable nouns ("The lion roared", "The lions roared") and with uncountable nouns when they refer to a specific example ("The rice we bought in the Thai shop is much better than the supermarket rice"). (3) We do not use a/an before uncountable nouns: "Could I have rice instead of potatoes with my fish?" (Not: "Could I have a rice"); "I hope we have nice weather" (Not: "I hope we have a nice weather").
